[Anthony Hopkins](Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins") and [Tatum O'Neal](Tatum_O'Neal "Tatum O'Neal") are the oldest and youngest winners of acting Oscars, winning at age 83 and age 10 respectively.

This is a list of oldest and youngest [Academy Award](Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") winners and nominees in the award categories Acting and Directing.

This list is based on "statistics valid through the nomination announcement for the [2015 (88th Academy Awards)](88th_Academy_Awards "88th Academy Awards"), announced on January 14, 2016", as documented in *The Official Academy Awards Database*.[[1]](List_of_oldest_and_youngest_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees#cite_note-AAD-1)

At the [90th Academy Awards](90th_Academy_Awards "90th Academy Awards"), [James Ivory](James_Ivory "James Ivory") became the oldest-ever Oscar winner in any category, at age 89, after receiving the award for [Best Adapted Screenplay](Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay") for his work on *[Call Me by Your Name](Call_Me_by_Your_Name_(film) "Call Me by Your Name (film)")*.[[2]](List_of_oldest_and_youngest_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees#cite_note-Wrap-2) At the [93rd Academy Awards](93rd_Academy_Awards "93rd Academy Awards"), [Ann Roth](Ann_Roth "Ann Roth") became the oldest-ever woman to win an Oscar in any category, at age 89, after receiving the award for [Best Costume Design](Academy_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design "Academy Award for Best Costume Design") for her work on *[Ma Rainey's Black Bottom](Ma_Rainey's_Black_Bottom_(film) "Ma Rainey's Black Bottom (film)")*.[[3]](List_of_oldest_and_youngest_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees#cite_note-LAT-3)

At the [95th Academy Awards](95th_Academy_Awards "95th Academy Awards"), [John Williams](John_Williams "John Williams") became the oldest Oscar nominee in any category, at age 90, after receiving his 53rd Oscar nomination for [Best Original Score](Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Academy Award for Best Original Score") for his work on *[The Fabelmans](The_Fabelmans "The Fabelmans")*.[[4]](List_of_oldest_and_youngest_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees#cite_note-Deadline-4)

There are only three people in Oscar history who have won two Oscars by the age of 30 or younger:

- [Luise Rainer](Luise_Rainer "Luise Rainer") for *[The Great Ziegfeld](The_Great_Ziegfeld "The Great Ziegfeld")* and [*The Good Earth*](The_Good_Earth_(film) "The Good Earth (film)")
- [Jodie Foster](Jodie_Foster "Jodie Foster") for *[The Accused](The_Accused_(1988_film) "The Accused (1988 film)")* and [*The Silence of the Lambs*](The_Silence_of_the_Lambs_(film) "The Silence of the Lambs (film)")
- [Hilary Swank](Hilary_Swank "Hilary Swank") for *[Boys Don't Cry](Boys_Don't_Cry_(1999_film) "Boys Don't Cry (1999 film)")* and *[Million Dollar Baby](Million_Dollar_Baby "Million Dollar Baby")*

This is a list of awards and nominations received by American director and screenwriter [Damien Chazelle](Damien_Chazelle "Damien Chazelle").

Chazelle made his directorial debut with the musical *[Guy and Madeline on a Park Bench](Guy_and_Madeline_on_a_Park_Bench "Guy and Madeline on a Park Bench")* (2009). He wrote and directed his second feature film, *[Whiplash](Whiplash_(2014_film) "Whiplash (2014 film)")* (2014), based on his award-winning [2013 short film of the same name](Whiplash_(2013_film) "Whiplash (2013 film)"). The film premiered at the [2014 Sundance Film Festival](2014_Sundance_Film_Festival "2014 Sundance Film Festival") as the opening film where it won the U.S. Grand Jury Prize: Dramatic and Audience Award: U.S. Dramatic and went on to receive five [Academy Award](87th_Academy_Awards "87th Academy Awards") nominations, including [Best Picture](Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), winning three with Chazelle himself nominated for [Best Adapted Screenplay](Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").

He is also known for co-writing *[10 Cloverfield Lane](10_Cloverfield_Lane "10 Cloverfield Lane")*, and writing and directing *[La La Land](La_La_Land_(film) "La La Land (film)")*, both released in 2016. For *La La Land*, he was nominated for several awards including two [Academy Awards](Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") for [Best Original Screenplay](Academy_Award "Academy Award") and [Best Director](Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"), [Directors Guild of America Award](Directors_Guild_of_America_Award "Directors Guild of America Award") for Best Director, [Writers Guild of America Award for Best Original Screenplay](Writers_Guild_of_America_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay "Writers Guild of America Award for Best Original Screenplay"), two [BAFTA Awards](BAFTA_Award "BAFTA Award") for [Best Original Screenplay](BAFTA_Award "BAFTA Award") and [Best Director](BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction") and won two [Critics' Choice Movie Award](Critics'_Choice_Movie_Award "Critics' Choice Movie Award") for [Best Screenplay](Critics'_Choice_Movie_Award "Critics' Choice Movie Award") and [Best Director](Critics'_Choice_Movie_Award_for_Best_Director "Critics' Choice Movie Award for Best Director") and also two [Golden Globe Award](Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award") for [Best Screenplay](Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award") and [Best Director](Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Director "Golden Globe Award for Best Director"), with the film itself receiving a record-breaking seven Golden Globes at the [74th Golden Globe Awards](74th_Golden_Globe_Awards "74th Golden Globe Awards").

At 32, Chazelle is the [youngest](List_of_oldest_and_youngest_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees#Youngest_winners "List of oldest and youngest Academy Award winners and nominees") person to win the Academy Award and Golden Globe Award for Best Director.[[1]](List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Damien_Chazelle#cite_note-youngest-1)[[2]](List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Damien_Chazelle#cite_note-youngestgg-2)

Milstein's family discouraged his early love of theater and his desire to follow the dramatic arts, and dispatched him to , [Saxony](Free_State_of_Saxony "Free State of Saxony"), to study engineering.[[4]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-4) After neglecting his classes to attend local theater productions, Milstein failed his coursework. He was intent on pursuing a theatrical career and bought a one-way ticket to the United States. In 1917, shortly after the US entered [World War I](World_War_I "World War I"), he enlisted in the [Signal Corps](Signal_Corps_(United_States_Army) "Signal Corps (United States Army)"). Milstein was stationed in New York City and Washington, D.C., and was assigned to the corps' photography unit, where he trained in aerial photography, assisted on training films and edited documentary combat footage. ### *Mutiny on the Bounty* (1962)

Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's remake of [Frank Lloyd](Frank_Lloyd "Frank Lloyd")'s 1935 film *[Mutiny on the Bounty](Mutiny_on_the_Bounty_(1935_film) "Mutiny on the Bounty (1935 film)")* starring [Clark Gable](Clark_Gable "Clark Gable") and [Charles Laughton](Charles_Laughton "Charles Laughton") was consistent with Hollywood's resort to blockbuster productions during the late Fifties. The studio risked over $20 million on the "ill-starred" 1962 *[Mutiny on the Bounty](Mutiny_on_the_Bounty_(1962_film) "Mutiny on the Bounty (1962 film)")* and recovered less than half of it.[[235]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-235)

In February 1961, the 65-year-old Milestone took over directorial duties from [Carol Reed](Carol_Reed "Carol Reed"), who became disillusioned with the project due to inadequate scripting, inclement weather on location in <Tahiti> and disputes with leading man [Marlon Brando](Marlon_Brando "Marlon Brando"). Milestone was tasked with bringing good order and discipline to the production, and with curbing Brando. Rather than inheriting a largely completed film, Milestone discovered only a few scenes had been filmed.[[236]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-236)

According to Miller (2010), the production history of the 1962 *Mutiny on the Bounty* is a record of personal and professional recriminations registered by Milestone and Brando rather than a coherent cinematic endeavor. To assert creative control over his character mutineer [Fletcher Christian](Fletcher_Christian "Fletcher Christian"), Brando collaborated with screenwriters and off the set, independently of Milestone, leading Milestone to withdraw from some scenes and sequences, and effectively relinquish control to Brando.[[237]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-237) Millichap refers to the film as "the Brando-Milestone" *Mutiny on the Bounty*, noting "the story of this Hollywood disaster is long and complex, but the central figure in every sense is Marlon Brando, not Lewis Milestone".[[238]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-238)

*Mutiny on the Bounty* is the final completed film for which Milestone was credited but according to Canham (1974), it is not considered representative of Milestone's *oeuvre*.[[239]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-239)

## Television and unrealized film projects: 1955–1965

After completing *[The Widow (La Vedova)](The_Widow_(1955_film) "The Widow (1955 film)")* (1955), Milestone returned to the United States in search of film projects. With the Hollywood studio system in decline, Milestone resorted to television to keep working. Five years elapsed before he completed another feature film.[[240]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-240)[[241]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-241) In 1956–1957, Milestone partnered with actor-producer [Kirk Douglas](Kirk_Douglas "Kirk Douglas"), who had debuted in Milestone's *[The Strange Love of Martha Ivers](The_Strange_Love_of_Martha_Ivers "The Strange Love of Martha Ivers")* (1946), to make a movie about a *[Citizen Kane](Citizen_Kane "Citizen Kane")*-like tycoon but the project, which was titled *King Kelly*, was abandoned after a year.[[242]](Lewis_Milestone#cite_note-242)

Upon its release, *7th Heaven* was a critical and commercial success and helped to establish Fox Film Corporation as a major studio. It was one of the first of three films to be nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Picture](Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture") (then called "Outstanding Picture") at the [1st Academy Awards](1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") held on May 16, 1929. In 1995, *7th Heaven* was selected for preservation in the United States [National Film Registry](National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry") by the [Library of Congress](Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".[[5]](7th_Heaven_(1927_film)#cite_note-5)[[6]](7th_Heaven_(1927_film)#cite_note-6) The film entered the [public domain](Public_domain "Public domain") in the United States in 2023.

## Plot

Chico works in the sewers of <Paris>. He dreams of becoming a street sweeper and therefore lights candles in the church. He also asks a blonde woman to be his partner. But his wishes are not granted, which makes him bitter.

One day Chico saves the young prostitute Diane, who is suffering from her unscrupulous sister Nana. The police want to arrest the prostitute, who is innocent in spite of her job, but Chico saves her by pretending to be her husband. Now the two have to maintain the facade and act as spouses. So Chico allows Diane to move into his attic with him. In fact, the two find each other. But when [the war breaks out](French_entry_into_World_War_I "French entry into World War I"), Chico is called up. Diane works in an ammunition factory. News of Chico's death reaches her, but Chico is not dead. He returns home to Diane, wounded and blind.

Their first child, Henry, was born in 1885. The Borzaga family moved to Salt Lake City, Utah, where Frank Borzage was born in 1894, and the family remained there until 1919. The couple had 14 children, eight of whom survived childhood: Henry (1885–1971), Mary Emma (1886–1906), Bill (1892–1973), Frank, Daniel (1896–1975, a performer and member of the [John Ford Stock Company](John_Ford_Stock_Company "John Ford Stock Company")), Lew (1898–1974), Dolly (1901–2002) and Sue (1905–1998). Luigi Borzaga died in Los Angeles in a car accident in 1934; his wife Maria (Frank's mother) died of cancer in 1947.

### Career

In 1912, Frank Borzage found employment as an actor in Hollywood; he continued to work as an actor until 1917. His directorial debut came in 1915 with the film *The Pitch o' Chance*.

Borzage was a successful director throughout the 1920s; he reached his peak in the late silent and early sound era. Absorbing visual influences from the German director [F.W. Murnau](F.W._Murnau "F.W. Murnau"), who was also resident at Fox at this time, he developed his own style of lushly visual romanticism in a hugely successful series of films starring [Janet Gaynor](Janet_Gaynor "Janet Gaynor") and [Charles Farrell](Charles_Farrell "Charles Farrell"), including *[7th Heaven](7th_Heaven_(1927_film) "7th Heaven (1927 film)")* (1927), for which he won the first [Academy Award for Best Director](Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director"),[[3]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-3) *[Street Angel](Street_Angel_(1928_film) "Street Angel (1928 film)")* (1928) and *[Lucky Star](Lucky_Star_(1929_film) "Lucky Star (1929 film)")* (1929). He won a second Oscar for 1931's *[Bad Girl](Bad_Girl_(1931_film) "Bad Girl (1931 film)")*.

He directed 14 films from 1917 to 1919 alone; his greatest success in the silent era was with *[Humoresque](Humoresque_(1920_film) "Humoresque (1920 film)")* (1920), a box-office winner starring [Vera Gordon](Vera_Gordon "Vera Gordon").[[4]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-4)[[5]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-5)

Borzage's trademark was intense identification with the feelings of young lovers in the face of adversity, with love in his films triumphing over such trials as World War I (*[7th Heaven](7th_Heaven_(1927_film) "7th Heaven (1927 film)")* and *[A Farewell to Arms](A_Farewell_to_Arms_(1932_film) "A Farewell to Arms (1932 film)")*), disability (*[Lucky Star](Lucky_Star_(1929_film) "Lucky Star (1929 film)")*), the Depression (*[Man's Castle](Man's_Castle "Man's Castle")*), a thinly disguised version of the [Titanic](RMS_Titanic "RMS Titanic") disaster in *[History Is Made at Night](History_Is_Made_at_Night_(1937_film) "History Is Made at Night (1937 film)")*, and the rise of <Nazism>, a theme which Borzage had virtually to himself among Hollywood filmmakers, including *[Little Man, What Now?](Little_Man%2C_What_Now%3F_(1934_film) "Little Man, What Now? (1934 film)")* (1933), *[Three Comrades](Three_Comrades_(1938_film) "Three Comrades (1938 film)")* (1938), and *[The Mortal Storm](The_Mortal_Storm "The Mortal Storm")* (1940).

His work took a spiritual turn in films such as *[Green Light](Green_Light_(1937_film) "Green Light (1937 film)")* (1937), *[Strange Cargo](Strange_Cargo_(1940_film) "Strange Cargo (1940 film)")* (1940) and *[The Big Fisherman](The_Big_Fisherman "The Big Fisherman")* (1959). Of his later work, only *[Moonrise](Moonrise_(film) "Moonrise (film)")* (1948) has enjoyed much critical acclaim.

After 1948, his output was sporadic, but he directed three episodes of the [[Screen Directors Playhouse]] series between 1955 and 1956.

In 1955 and 1957, Borzage was awarded The George Eastman Award, given by [George Eastman House](George_Eastman_House "George Eastman House") for distinguished contribution to the art of film.[[6]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-6) For his contributions to the film industry, Borzage received a [motion pictures star](List_of_actors_with_Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame_motion_picture_stars "List of actors with Hollywood Walk of Fame motion picture stars") on the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame") in 1960. The star is located at 6300 Hollywood Boulevard.[[7]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-7)

He was the original director of *[Journey Beneath the Desert](Journey_Beneath_the_Desert "Journey Beneath the Desert")* (1961), but was too unwell to continue, and [Edgar G. Ulmer](Edgar_G._Ulmer "Edgar G. Ulmer") took over.[[8]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-8) Borzage was uncredited for the sequences he did direct.

While hospitalized in February 1962, he received the [D. W. Griffith Award](D._W._Griffith_Award "D. W. Griffith Award").[[9]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-9)

He was an officer and board member of the [Directors Guild of America](Directors_Guild_of_America "Directors Guild of America").[[10]](Frank_Borzage#cite_note-dvobit-10)
